units.translation: For I have made it clearer with my eyes.
So that I may speak more clearly as one who knows.
And the house itself, if it could find a voice, would speak most clearly.
reverence, awe, majesty
reverence, adoration, sanctity.
one who is revered or worshipped.

which the scholiast understood as referring to reverence toward Agamemnon: ἑκούσιον σέβας [voluntary reverence] is that which arises for them not from fear but from respect. This means that the respect which the people had for Agamemnon has now turned to fear. For they revered and loved him, but they fear this man as a tyrant. More correctly Schuetz took σέβας [reverence] as referring to Agamemnon's majesty itself.
where Orestes is said to be σέβας φέρων [bringing reverence] to his sister Electra: for which Schuetz conjectured σέλας φέρων [bringing light].

which the scholiast took as σέβας ὄντι [being an object of reverence] when he interpreted it as ἐπ᾿ ἀνδρὶ φοβερῷ καὶ σεβαστῷ καὶ παρὰ τοῖς πολεμίοις [upon a man feared and revered even among enemies], which could not be said in this way, nor, if it could, would it be fitting, since Agamemnon was to be feared by enemies but revered by his own people, as was said above at line 53. No more probable is Heimsoeth's interpretation on p. 246, who, placing a punctuation before ἐπ᾿ ἀνδρὶ [upon a man], took σέβας [reverence] as standing for σέβας ἔστι or ἔπεστι [there is reverence]. For the words ἐπ᾿ ἀνδρὶ [upon a man] clearly cohere with the preceding γυναικοβούλους τε μήτιδας φρενών [woman-counselling devices of the mind]. The opinions of scholars about the emendation and interpretation of this strophe are most diverse, among which Hermann's conjecture is memorable: he removed the suspect word σέβας [reverence], which could not stand for σέβας ὄντι [being an object of reverence], by writing ἄκαιρος δ᾽ ὁ δυσφιλές σέβων, τίων τ᾽ ἀθέρμαντον ἑστίαν δόμων, γυναικείαν τ᾽ ἄτολμον αἰχμάν [untimely is he who reveres what is hateful, and honors the cold hearth of the house, and the cowardly spear of a woman], to which the second participle τίων δ᾽ [and honoring] is suited (for thus M), for which Stanley had written τίω δ᾽ [and I honor]. The verb σέβειν [to revere] recurs in the antistrophic line 637: σέβει γὰρ οὔτις τὸ δυσφιλές θεοῖς [for no one reveres what is hateful to the gods].

where the scholiast says: τὸ τῶν ἱκετῶν σέβισμα [the reverence of suppliants] (the usual form is σέβασμα) καὶ δέημα [and their prayer] not only does Zeus honor, but also reveres, seeing it set in motion with fitting fortune.
where the use of the plural σέβη [reverences] is to be noted, of which no other example is found: for this reason Conington conjectured ἕδη [seats], Nauck στέφη [garlands].
And the awe, unconquerable, untamed, unwarlike, that once passed through the ears and the mind of the people, now departs.
And you were a faithful brother to me, bringing reverence.
Upon a man bearing arms, upon a man wrathful against enemies, reverence.
Having transgressed all reverence for Zeus.
Zeus indeed reveres this reverence of the lawless.
Honoring well the reverence of parents.
Fearing such reverence justly.
Fearing these tridents and the reverences of the gods.
And you did not respect the holy reverence of my thighs.
And in it reverence of citizens and kindred fear will hold back injustice.
If the reverence of Persuasion is holy to you.
Reverence of the gods.
Judge the reverence due to the gods.
For the reverence of parents is written third in the ordinances of Justice.
O reverence of my mother.
